research.interest: Tracking the sets and MOCs I build bag by bag and what happens to each one afterwards
research.desired_outcome: Always know which build is on the bench, which bag I stopped on, and which parts I am short before I sit down again
practice: Open a set and work through its numbered bags over several sittings, stopping mid-step when the evening runs out
Build a MOC that has no set number, no numbered bags, and no official piece count, only a designer and a count I trust
Decide what happens to a finished build — it goes on the display shelf, stays boxed, or gets parted out into the bins
Notice a missing or lost piece mid-build and keep it on a list until an order is worth placing
constraints: capture happens at the mat with parts in both hands
a MOC must be as first-class as an official set
part numbers and piece counts keep the catalogue's own values
open_questions: whether minifigs are tracked apart from their sets
whether parted-out sets stay in the collection
how much of the loose parts library is worth cataloguing
usage_context: phone beside the build mat mid-sitting
desktop when planning an order or rearranging the shelf
research.first_value: Log one sitting against one set and see the bag you stopped on waiting for you next time

evidence.claim: Serious LEGO tracking keeps the official set as canonical identity addressed by set number, separate from the builder's own copy of it.
Parts and colours are first-class records addressed by part number and colour rather than free text on a set, and MOCs are catalogued beside official sets.
Stable identities and relationships should be explicit and enforceable rather than repeated as text fields.
A build sitting is an activity against a project; corrections preserve the original log rather than overwriting it.
Indexes should follow concrete filtering, joining, and ordering workloads.
Global and local example-driven alternatives support meaningful concept exploration and remix.
Begin with user needs and real context, then do the hard work required to make the service simple.
Keyboard access, focus, reflow, labels, status, and error recovery are release requirements.

concepts.title: The Shelf Run
concepts.thesis: Make the finished collection the interface and keep building a light annotation on top of it.
concepts.primary_loop: Add a set to the collection, mark it finished, and browse the shelf by theme and year.
concepts.primary_affordance: A stud-grid shelf run where every finished build takes the width of its own footprint
concepts.differentiator: Fastest way to answer what is already built and what the collection is missing
tradeoffs: work in progress is invisible between sittings
missing parts have nowhere to live

concepts.title: Build Bench
concepts.thesis: Anchor the app on the build that is open right now and make resuming it the cheapest thing you can do.
concepts.primary_loop: Open tonight's build, finish a couple of bags, and log the step you stopped on before the parts go away.
concepts.primary_affordance: An instruction-step progress strip above the open build's sitting log
concepts.differentiator: The only concept that answers which bag am I on without a search
feature_boundary: sitting capture with bags and steps
tradeoffs: parts analysis arrives only after sittings accumulate

concepts.title: Parts Ledger
concepts.thesis: Treat every missing and spare element as inventory and let completion be a number rather than a feeling.
concepts.primary_loop: Record what is short or spare, watch completion percentages move, and export one order list.
concepts.primary_affordance: A parts-bin drawer wall with a completion meter on every build
concepts.differentiator: Turns scattered missing-piece notes into a single order and a real inventory
tradeoffs: needs disciplined part numbering before it pays off
capture is heavier at the mat

user_decisions: A MOC is a first-class project — it has no set number but it still has a build log
Parting a set out is a normal end of life and not a deletion

relationships.description: A project that follows an official set names it once by set number; a MOC names none.
Every sitting belongs to exactly one build project.
A shortage is always short for one particular build.
A build lives in one physical place at a time.

constraints.reason: A catalogued set has pieces and never a negative minifig count.
A shortage records at least one missing piece and stays within a plausible order.
A sitting that took no time at the mat did not happen.
One label per physical place so bins and shelves cannot quietly drift apart.
A build cannot be displayed before it is built and cannot be un-parted once its bricks are in the bins.

indexes.reason: The bench filters to work in progress in the order each build was started.
A build's sittings are read in order every time it is resumed.
One order list groups open shortages by part number across every build at once.
The shelf run is browsed by theme and then by release year.

workloads.question: What is on the bench right now and which bag am I on?
workloads.expected_scale: fewer than ten builds open at once
workloads.acceptance: Every open build shows its last bag, its step, and how long ago it was touched without a query.

workloads.question: What is on the display shelf and how does the collection group by theme and year?
workloads.expected_scale: hundreds of builds across a decade
workloads.acceptance: Displayed builds group by theme with piece count and stud footprint visible beside each one.

workloads.question: Which parts am I short across every build and what should the next order contain?
workloads.expected_scale: hundreds of shortages over the collection's life
workloads.acceptance: Open shortages group by part number and colour with the build each one belongs to and no build is double-counted.

workloads.question: How many sittings and hours did this build take compared with the last one of its size?
workloads.expected_scale: dozens of sittings for a large set
workloads.acceptance: Sittings line up chronologically with minutes and bags so pace is comparable between builds of similar piece counts.

visual_world.name: Instruction Bench
visual_world.mood: Bright and precise and unhurried — an instruction booklet open on a clean grey mat
visual_world.typography: A geometric sans for set names and step numbers with a monospaced face for part numbers and piece counts
visual_world.color_strategy: Mat grey and page white with a technical callout blue for the step in progress and a moss green counterpoint for finished work; no primary-colour brand cosplay and no toy-aisle saturation
visual_world.layout_principle: The open build holds the top of the page and the shelf and the bins unfold beneath it as evidence rather than as a dashboard grid
visual_world.density: Spacious while a sitting is being logged and tight and aligned when scanning part numbers
signature_elements: a stud-grid rail that measures a build's progress in studs rather than a percentage bar
an instruction-step progress strip showing the bag you are on and the bags still sealed
parts-bin drawer cards that open into the shortages they hold
a shelf run where each finished build takes the width of its own stud footprint

views.title: The Build Bench
views.purpose: Show what is open right now and log where this sitting stopped before the parts are put away.
views.layout: The open build holds the stage with its sitting log beside it; anything flagged short this evening lands underneath.

actions.label: Log this sitting
actions.consequence: Records the bags finished, the step reached, and the minutes spent at the mat.

actions.label: Flag a part short
actions.consequence: Files the part number, the colour, and the count short without leaving the step.

actions.label: Mark it built
actions.consequence: Moves the build off the bench so it can be shelved or parted out.

actions.label: Correct a sitting
actions.consequence: Keeps the original log and records the correction beside it.

views.title: Shelf Run
views.purpose: See what is finished and on display and how the collection reads by theme.
views.layout: Finished builds run across the shelf at their own stud footprints with the selected set's catalogue facts in an inspector margin.

actions.label: Add a build
actions.consequence: Puts a sealed set or a new MOC on the bench with its origin, set number, and designer recorded honestly.

actions.label: Put it on the shelf
actions.consequence: Moves a finished build into a display slot and records its stud footprint.

actions.label: Rename a place
actions.consequence: Renames a shelf or a bin without breaking the builds that point at it.

views.title: Parts Ledger
views.purpose: Turn every part flagged short into one order and remember which bin the parted-out bricks went into.
views.layout: The order list leads as a dense table; the bins that already hold sorted parts sit beside it as drawer cards.

actions.label: Mark ordered
actions.consequence: Moves the shortage out of the next order without deleting the observation.

actions.label: Show the build behind this
actions.consequence: Opens the build and the sitting where the part came up short.

views.title: Build Pace
views.purpose: Compare how long a build actually took against the last one of its size.
views.layout: Minutes per sitting draw the pace across the stage with a comparison of builds aligned beneath it.

actions.label: Show the sittings behind this

flows.title: Log the first real sitting
flows.trigger: User approves the Build Bench concept.

steps.action: Name the set or the MOC, then say which bags were finished and which step it stopped on.
steps.result: A sitting receipt appears against that build with the bag and the step preserved.

steps.action: Confirm or correct the interpreted bags and minutes.
steps.result: The canonical sitting and its provenance are visible in the build's log.

flows.success: The builder can point at tonight's sitting and see exactly where to resume next time.

flows.title: Take a build from the last bag to the shelf
flows.trigger: The final numbered bag of a set is finished.

steps.result: It leaves the bench and waits for a place to live.

steps.action: Choose a display slot and record the stud footprint.
steps.result: The build joins the shelf run under its own theme.

flows.success: The finished build is on the shelf and the bench shows only work that is still open.

flows.title: Turn flagged shortages into one order
flows.trigger: Two or more builds are waiting on missing parts.

steps.action: Group open shortages by part number and colour.
steps.result: One order list covers every waiting build at once.
The observations stay intact while the order is out.

flows.success: Nothing is ordered twice and no build is quietly forgotten while it waits for two tiles.

responsive_strategy: On phones the open build and its Log a sitting action take the first screen and the shelf run becomes a swipeable rail with the parts ledger paged horizontally.
On desktop the bench keeps the open build and its sittings side by side and the parts ledger gains a full sortable table with part numbers aligned.

cases.expected: They remain distinct build projects with independent statuses, sittings, and shortages while sharing one canonical set record.

cases.input: A MOC is created with no set number and a hand-counted 3800 pieces.
cases.expected: The project is accepted with its designer and claimed piece count, and no canonical set is invented to hold it.

release_thresholds.schema: all identity, relationship, constraint, and state-transition cases pass
release_thresholds.experience: first sitting and finish-and-shelve flows pass on mobile and desktop
release_thresholds.evidence: every entity and critical view has an approved derivation

derivations.decision: Separate the catalogued set, the builder's copy, the sitting, the shortage, and the place it lives so identity, ownership, activity, observation, and storage each keep their own lifecycle.
Make origin an explicit enum so a MOC is a first-class project with a designer and a claimed piece count instead of an official set number that does not exist.
derivations.user_decision: A MOC is a first-class project — it has no set number but it still has a build log.

derivations.decision: Model parting out as a legal end state rather than a deletion, because a parted-out set still explains where its bricks went.
derivations.user_decision: Parting a set out is a normal end of life and not a deletion.

derivations.decision: Anchor the app on the build in progress and the bag it stopped on rather than on the finished collection, because capture happens at the mat with parts in both hands.
derivations.user_decision: Logging where I stopped has to take one action with parts in both hands.

derivations.decision: Index shortages by status and part number so one order list can cover every waiting build at once.
Use an instruction-booklet world with a stud-grid progress rail instead of a kanban board or toy-aisle colour, so the app reads as documentation of a build rather than a shop.
